title: Database Management Systems (DBMS)
overview: A DBMS is the software through which every user and program reaches a database. This topic covers the DBMS features that fix the problems of a file-based approach (data management through a data dictionary, data modelling, the logical schema, data integrity, and data security through backup procedures and access rights for individuals and groups) and the software tools a DBMS provides in practice: the developer interface and the query processor. Paper 1 questions typically ask you to name a feature and explain the file-based problem it solves, describe what a data dictionary holds, or explain how access rights and backups protect the data in a given scenario.
syllabusPoints: Show understanding of the features provided by a Database Management System (DBMS) that address the issues of a file-based approach, including data management (maintaining a data dictionary), data modelling and the logical schema.
Show understanding of the features provided by a DBMS that address the issues of a file-based approach, including data integrity.

Show understanding of the features provided by a DBMS that address the issues of a file-based approach, including data security: backup procedures and the use of access rights for individuals / groups of users.
Show understanding of how software tools found within a DBMS are used in practice, including the use and purpose of the developer interface.
Show understanding of how software tools found within a DBMS are used in practice, including the use and purpose of the query processor.

definitions.definition: Software that controls all access to the data in a database: it creates and maintains the structure, stores and retrieves data on request, and enforces integrity and security rules.
The person who uses the DBMS to set up and customise the database for its users, including defining views and access rights and organising backups.

A part of the database, maintained by the DBMS and visible only to the DBA, holding metadata (data about the data): table and attribute names, data types, keys, relationships, validation rules, indexes, access rights and physical storage details.
Analysing an organisation's data to identify its entities, attributes and relationships, typically as an E-R diagram, so the structure can be defined in the DBMS.

The overall description of how the database is organised as seen by users and programmers (its tables, attributes, keys, relationships and constraints), independent of how the data is physically stored. Also called the conceptual schema.
The accuracy, completeness and consistency of the stored data, maintained by the DBMS through keys, referential integrity, validation rules and controlled updates.
Permissions assigned by the DBA to an individual user or a group of users stating which tables or views they can reach and whether they can read, insert, update or delete data.
A copy of the database made at regular, planned intervals and stored separately from the live data, so the database can be restored if the original is lost or corrupted.
The part of a DBMS giving developers access to tools for creating tables, defining attributes, data types and keys, and building forms, queries and reports.
The DBMS software that accepts a query, checks it against the data dictionary, turns it into an efficient plan and executes it to retrieve or change the data.

sections.title: The DBMS and the problems it solves
content: A database is more than a collection of files: it is data organised according to a model (for AS, the relational model) and managed by a database management system. Programs and users never read or write the stored data directly; they send requests to the DBMS, which carries out the operation and applies the same rules every time. This single controlling layer is what solves the problems of the file-based approach. Data is held once and shared by every department instead of each department keeping its own copy, which removes redundancy and inconsistency. Structure is defined once, centrally, in the data dictionary, instead of inside each program. Validation, key and relationship rules are enforced whoever enters the data. Access is controlled per user or group rather than being all-or-nothing for a file. Backups are organised centrally by the database administrator (DBA) instead of being left to chance. The syllabus groups these features as data management, data modelling, the logical schema, data integrity and data security.
bullets: Every create, read, update and delete request passes through the DBMS, so rules are applied consistently.
The DBA is the person who uses the DBMS to set up the database, user views, access rights and backup routines.
Examples of relational DBMS software include MySQL, PostgreSQL, Microsoft Access and Microsoft SQL Server.

sections.title: Data modelling
content: Before a database is built its data must be modelled: the designer identifies the entities the organisation needs to store data about, their attributes and the relationships between them, usually drawn as an E-R diagram (see 8.1). The first model is conceptual, describing the data without reference to any particular technology. It is then turned into a logical model for a relational database, where each entity becomes a table, many-to-many relationships are resolved with link tables, and primary and foreign keys are chosen. Many DBMSs include modelling tools that let the designer draw tables and relationship lines, and then generate the table definitions directly from the diagram, or show the relationships between existing tables. This is a feature a file-based approach lacks: there, the structure of each file is decided separately by each program's author, with no overall model of how the data fits together.
bullets: Data modelling produces the entities, attributes, relationships and keys that the logical schema records.
A good model is what makes normalised, non-redundant tables possible.
DBMS relationship tools let the designer declare foreign keys so that referential integrity is then enforced automatically.

sections.title: The logical schema and data independence
content: A DBMS describes a database at three levels. At the internal level, the internal schema records how the data is physically stored on disk; only the DBMS software deals with this. At the conceptual level there is a single logical schema: the complete description of the database as users and programmers understand it, meaning every table, attribute, data type, key, relationship and constraint, with no mention of physical storage. The DBA controls this level. At the external level, each user group or program has its own view (external schema) showing only the part of the database it needs; for example, a finance view might include member payments but not coaching notes. Separating the levels gives data independence. If the physical storage is reorganised or moved to new hardware, the logical schema is unchanged, so programs keep working. If a new attribute or table is added to the logical schema, existing views and the programs that use them are unaffected, and only new programs that need the new data have to be written. This is the direct fix for the data dependency problem of file-based systems.
bullets: Logical schema = what data is held and how it is organised; internal schema = how it is stored physically.
External views are also a security mechanism, because a user can only reach the data in their view.
Data independence means changes at one level do not force changes to programs working at a higher level.

sections.title: Data security: access rights for individuals and groups
content: In a file-based system anyone who can open a file can read all of it. A DBMS lets the DBA control access at a much finer level. Each person logs in with their own user account, authenticated by a password or similar, so the DBMS knows who is making every request. The DBA then assigns access rights, which state which tables or views the account can use and which operations are allowed on each: read (SELECT), insert, update or delete. Rather than setting rights one person at a time, users with the same job are usually placed in a group (or role), such as Reception, Finance or Coaches, and the rights are granted to the group; a new employee then only needs to be added to the right group, and a change of job means moving them to another group. Individual rights can still be added or removed where one person needs something different, such as a manager who can delete records. Following the principle of least privilege, each user or group receives only the access their work requires, which protects confidential data and limits the damage from mistakes or a compromised account.
bullets: Authentication (user ID and password) establishes who the user is; access rights then decide what that user may do.
Rights can be limited to particular tables, to views that hide some attributes, and to particular operations.
Group rights make administration simpler and more consistent than setting every user's rights separately.
The DBMS can also keep an audit log of who accessed or changed which data.

examples.label: Access rights by group for a sports centre database
examples.content:
Group | Member | ClassMember | Payment | Instructor
Reception | read, insert, update | read, insert, delete | none | read
Finance | read | read | read, insert, update | none
Coaches | read (view without phone numbers) | read | none | read
DBA | full | full | full | full

A receptionist can enrol a member in a class but cannot see or alter payment records; a coach sees who is in a class without seeing members' contact details.

sections.title: Software tools: the developer interface
content: The developer interface is the part of the DBMS that gives developers the tools to build and change a database. Through it a developer creates tables, names each attribute and sets its data type and size, declares the primary key and foreign keys (which records the relationships and switches on referential integrity), adds validation rules such as a range check or a required field, and creates indexes. The same interface is used to build the parts that end users see: data-entry forms, saved queries and formatted reports, which can be combined into a user interface so staff can work with the data without knowing SQL. Most DBMSs offer both a graphical way of doing this (design grids, drag-and-drop form designers, query-by-example) and a way to type SQL commands directly. Graphical tools are quicker for simple tasks, while writing SQL gives the developer precise control and is needed for more complex queries; in either case the DBMS ultimately carries out the work using its DDL and DML (see 8.3).
bullets: Used for: creating and altering tables, attributes, data types, keys, validation rules and indexes.
Also used for: designing forms for data entry, queries for retrieving data and reports for presenting output.
Every change to the structure made here is recorded in the data dictionary.

sections.title: Software tools: the query processor
content: A query is a request to select data that meets stated conditions, or to change data. The query processor is the DBMS software that accepts a query, whether typed in SQL or built with a graphical query tool, and carries it out. It first checks the query: that it is correctly formed, that every table and attribute named exists (by looking them up in the data dictionary) and that the user has the access rights needed. It then works out an efficient way of executing it, for example deciding to use an index on a key attribute rather than scanning a whole table, or choosing the order in which to join tables. Finally it executes the plan against the stored data and returns the result, such as a table of matching rows, or makes the requested changes. Structure-changing (DDL) statements are handled by updating the data dictionary; data-handling (DML) statements are compiled and run against the tables. Because users only describe what data they want, not how to find it, the same query keeps working even if the physical storage or indexes change.
bullets: Purpose: allow queries to be created and executed so data can be extracted or updated.
Steps: check syntax and names against the data dictionary, check access rights, optimise, execute, return the result.
Query results can be used directly, fed into a report, or built into a form in the user interface.

examples.label: How the query processor handles one query
examples.content:
Query from a receptionist:
SELECT MemberName FROM Member WHERE MemberID = 'M104';

1. Parse: the statement is valid SQL.
2. Check names: the data dictionary confirms table Member and attributes MemberName, MemberID exist, and MemberID is VARCHAR so 'M104' is a valid comparison.
3. Check rights: the Reception group has read access to Member.
4. Optimise: MemberID is the primary key and has an index, so use the index instead of reading every row.
5. Execute: follow the index pointer to the M104 row.
6. Return: MemberName = O. Haddad.

sections.title: Data management: the data dictionary
content: Data management in a DBMS is centred on the data dictionary: a part of the database, maintained by the DBMS and normally hidden from everyone except the DBA, that holds metadata, meaning data about the data rather than the data itself. It stores the name of every table, the name, data type and size of every attribute, primary and foreign keys and the relationships they form, validation rules and default values, indexes, user views and access rights, and details of how the data is physically stored. The DBMS keeps it up to date automatically whenever the structure is changed through the developer interface or a DDL command, and consults it constantly: the query processor uses it to check that names in a query exist and to find indexes, and the data-entry process uses it to check each new value against its data type and validation rule. In a file-based system this information is scattered inside each program; in a DBMS it is held once and shared, so every program works to the same definitions.
bullets: Metadata examples to quote: table names, attribute names, data types, field lengths, primary/foreign keys, validation rules, relationships, access rights.
The data dictionary does not contain the records themselves (for example, not a member's actual phone number).
Because definitions are central, a change such as lengthening an attribute is made once and applies to every program.

examples.label: Part of the data dictionary for the Member table
examples.content:
Table: Member
Attribute | Data type | Size | Key | Validation
MemberID | VARCHAR | 4 | Primary key | Format: letter M followed by 3 digits
MemberName | VARCHAR | 40 | - | Required
MemberPhone | VARCHAR | 15 | - | -
EmailAddress | VARCHAR | 60 | Secondary key (indexed) | Must be unique
Indexes: MemberID, EmailAddress
Referenced by: ClassMember.MemberID (foreign key)

sections.title: Data integrity
content: Data integrity means the stored data is accurate, complete and consistent. A DBMS maintains it with several features that a file-based approach lacks. Entity integrity: every table has a primary key and the DBMS rejects a missing or duplicate key value, so no tuple is recorded twice. Referential integrity: a foreign key value is accepted only if it matches an existing primary key in the referenced table, and a referenced tuple cannot be deleted while others still depend on it. Validation: each value is checked against the data type, size and any rule held in the data dictionary (a range check on a price, a format check on an ID, a presence check on a required attribute). Single storage: because each fact is held once, there are no copies to fall out of step. Controlled updates: a transaction that is interrupted part way, for example by a power failure, is either completed or fully undone, so the database is never left half-updated, and when several users update at the same time the DBMS uses record locking so one user's change cannot silently overwrite another's.
bullets: Validation reduces errors but cannot guarantee correctness: a valid but wrong phone number will still be accepted.
Keys and referential integrity are declared once in the DBMS and then enforced for every program and user.
Record locking stops two users updating the same tuple at once, preventing a lost update.

sections.title: Data security: backup procedures
content: Access rights protect data from people who should not see or change it, but they do not protect against hardware failure, accidental deletion, corruption, malware or a fire in the server room. For that, the DBA sets up a backup procedure, and the DBMS provides tools to run it, often automatically. A good procedure states what is copied, how often, where the copies are kept, how long they are kept and how they are tested. A common pattern is a full backup of the whole database at regular intervals (for example, every night when few users are working) with incremental backups of only the changes in between. Copies are stored off-site or in the cloud, and often encrypted, so that the event that damages the live system cannot also destroy the backups, and several generations are kept in case the most recent copy is itself corrupted. Many DBMSs also keep a transaction log of every change since the last backup. To recover, the latest backup is restored and the logged transactions are reapplied, bringing the database back to its state just before the failure. Restores should be tested regularly, because a backup that cannot be restored gives no protection.
bullets: Backup frequency is set by how much data the organisation can afford to lose: data changed since the last backup (and not in a log) is lost.
Store backups away from the live database, for example off-site or in the cloud.
Keep several generations of backups, and test that they can actually be restored.
A transaction log lets recovery go beyond the last backup up to the point of failure.

examples.label: Recovering after a disk failure
examples.content:
Procedure: full backup every night at 01:00 to an encrypted cloud store; 14 nightly copies kept; transaction log kept on a separate disk.

The server disk fails at 15:30 on Thursday.
1. Replace the disk and restore Thursday's 01:00 full backup: the database is now as it was at 01:00.
2. Reapply the transaction log from 01:00 to 15:30: all changes made during Thursday are restored.
3. Only transactions still in progress at 15:30 are lost.
Without the log, every change made between 01:00 and 15:30 would have been lost.

comparisonTable.title: File-based problems and the DBMS features that address them
rows: Structure hidden inside each program; files defined separately
All table, attribute, type and key definitions are held once as metadata and shared by every program
No overall plan of how the data fits together
Entities, attributes and relationships are designed as one model and implemented as linked tables
Programs depend on file layout; structure changes force rewrites
Programs work with the logical structure, so physical or additional changes do not break them (data independence)
Redundant copies, duplicates, no checks on entry
Data stored once; primary keys, referential integrity and validation rules enforced for every entry
Anyone who opens a file can read all of it
Individual and group rights control which tables or views each user may read or change
Scheduled, off-site, tested backups plus a transaction log allow full recovery

diagram.title: Three-level view of a database managed by a DBMS
nodes: External level: user and program views (each with its own access rights)
Conceptual level: the logical schema, controlled by the DBA
DBMS software: developer interface, query processor, data dictionary
Internal level: internal schema and physical storage on disk

analysisChains.title: Adding a new attribute without breaking existing programs
steps: The sports centre decides to record an emergency contact for each member
The developer adds the attribute EmergencyContact to Member through the developer interface
The DBMS updates the data dictionary and the logical schema; existing views are unchanged
Existing reception and finance programs continue to run, and only a new form is written to capture the new data
analysisChains.evaluation: This is data independence in practice. In a file-based system the file layout and every program reading it would have had to be rewritten.

analysisChains.title: Using groups to manage access rights
steps: Reception staff need to enrol members; finance staff need to record payments; coaches only need class lists
The DBA creates a group for each role and grants rights to tables or views per group
A new receptionist is added to the Reception group and immediately has exactly the right access
When a coach moves to finance, the DBA moves the account between groups rather than editing individual rights
analysisChains.evaluation: Group rights are quicker to manage and less error-prone than per-user rights, and they apply least privilege so confidential data such as payments is seen only by those who need it.

analysisChains.title: Why backups must be stored off-site
steps: The centre backs up nightly to a second disk inside the same server
A fire destroys the server room
Both the live database and every backup copy are lost at the same time
analysisChains.evaluation: A backup only protects against events that cannot also reach it. Storing copies off-site or in the cloud, keeping several generations and testing restores make the backup procedure effective.

examTips: For 'describe a feature of a DBMS that addresses a file-based limitation', give the feature, the limitation and the link: 'the data dictionary holds all attribute definitions once, so programs no longer each define the file structure'.
When asked what a data dictionary contains, give concrete metadata items (attribute names, data types, field lengths, primary keys, validation rules), never actual data values.
For access rights, mention both individuals and groups and name the type of access (read-only, read/write, delete, no access) for specific tables or views in the scenario.
For backup procedures, cover frequency, full versus incremental, storage off-site or in the cloud, keeping several copies and testing the restore.
Distinguish the two software tools: the developer interface is for building the database and its forms and reports; the query processor is for creating and executing queries.
commonMistakes: Saying the data dictionary stores the data; it stores metadata about the structure of the data.
Confusing the logical schema (what data is held and how it is organised) with physical storage (how it is held on disk).
Treating access rights as the same as passwords; a password authenticates the user, access rights decide what that user can do.
Describing a backup as 'saving the data' without saying it is a separate copy, made regularly and stored away from the live database.
Calling the query processor 'where you type SQL'; it checks, optimises and executes queries, whatever interface was used to create them.
Listing DBMS features without linking each one to the file-based problem it solves when the question asks for that link.

quickRecall.question: What is a data dictionary? Give two items it holds.
quickRecall.answer: A part of the database holding metadata (data about the data). Any two of: table names, attribute names, data types, field lengths, primary/foreign keys, validation rules, relationships, indexes, access rights.

quickRecall.question: What is the logical schema?
quickRecall.answer: The overall description of the database as seen by users and programmers: its tables, attributes, keys, relationships and constraints, independent of physical storage.

quickRecall.question: How does a DBMS maintain data integrity?
quickRecall.answer: Through primary keys (no duplicate or missing keys), referential integrity on foreign keys, validation rules from the data dictionary, storing each fact once, and controlled updates such as record locking.

quickRecall.question: Why are access rights often given to groups rather than individuals?
quickRecall.answer: Users with the same job need the same access, so granting rights to a group is quicker and more consistent; new or moving staff just join the appropriate group.

quickRecall.question: Give three features of a good backup procedure.
quickRecall.answer: Any three of: regular scheduled backups (full and incremental), stored off-site or in the cloud, encrypted, several generations kept, restores tested, transaction log kept to recover up to the failure.

quickRecall.question: What is the developer interface used for?
quickRecall.answer: Creating and altering tables, attributes, data types, keys, validation rules and indexes, and building forms, queries and reports for the user interface.

quickRecall.question: What does the query processor do?
quickRecall.answer: Accepts a query, checks it against the data dictionary and the user's rights, works out an efficient way to run it (for example using an index) and executes it to return or change data.
